To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
alcohol and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection cause methylation defects that contribute to liver disease.
the methylation defects in ALD and HCV are linked to proteasome function and IFN signaling, and these defects can be corrected by betaine or S-adenoslymethionine to improve liver injury.

EtOH and viral infection impair methylation reactions to disrupt cytokine signaling and antigen presentation in the hepatocytes, as well as to alter TNFα expression and proteasome activity in the macrophages.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how EtOH and viral proteins disrupt methylation reactions and the consequences of this disruption on liver disease pathogenesis.
the impact of altered methylation reactions on cytokine signaling pathways in viral and alcoholic liver diseases.
the impact of altered methylation on liver disease and the therapeutic potential of correcting methylation reactions to treat ALD and viral hepatitis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the methylation defects in ALD, viral infection, and the interaction of the two are a major contributor to the pathogenesis of the disease and can be reversed by therapeutic intervention.
the methylation reaction is a key regulator of many cellular pathways that are disrupted in ALD and HCV infection.
methylation defects contribute to the severity of viral-mediated liver injury, which may be overcome with therapeutic agents that correct methylation defects.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the presence of alcohol and/or virus alters methylation and proteasome functions to disrupt the immune response in the liver, thereby exacerbating the severity of the liver disease.
EtOH and HCV synergistically impair methylation reactions that promote the pathophysiology of ALD.

EtOH-induced methylation defects contribute to the severity of viral-induced liver injury, and the use of methylation precursors could be a novel therapeutic approach for treating ALD and viral hepatitis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the methylation defects are an important contributor to ALD pathogenesis.
the presence of EtOH and/or viral proteins can disrupt multiple methylation-dependent signaling pathways that are important for liver disease progression.
the combination of alcohol and hepatitis C virus infection leads to multiple defects in methylation reactions that impair the immune response and promote the progression of liver injury.
